strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of MAPPO limitations (critic instability, computational overhead) in LLM-based multi-agent systems
Comprehensive empirical analysis within experimental scope including detailed training dynamics, convergence behavior, and resource consumption measurements
Practical improvements demonstrated: MHGPO variants outperform MAPPO on HotpotQA (~2.6% accuracy gain) with substantially lower GPU memory (57-82% vs 100%)
Insightful analysis of why heterogeneous groups work: empirical demonstration that they naturally converge to homogeneous groups during training (Figures 7-9)
Three well-articulated sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR) representing meaningful efficiency-effectiveness trade-offs with clear algorithmic specification
High quality presentation with clear figures, detailed algorithms, and comprehensive case study demonstrating qualitative improvements
Sound technical approach with correctly derived equations and well-specified algorithms
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily adapts existing group-based optimization methods (GRPO/DAPO) to multi-agent settings; the main contribution (Eq. 5) is a straightforward extension

Severely narrow experimental scope: only one MAS type (three-agent sequential pipeline), one primary LLM (Llama3.1-8B), one task domain (multi-hop QA); yet claims generalization to 'all MAS' unsupported by evidence
Weak baseline comparison: only MAPPO tested; notably missing comparison to DAPO despite being mentioned; no comparison to other critic-free MARL approaches
Modest performance improvements lacking statistical significance: HotpotQA +2.6%, 2WikiMultihopQA +1.05%, MuSiQue -0.25% regression; no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported
Limited training protocol: only one epoch of training may not reveal long-term dynamics; single epoch may bias results toward faster-converging methods (FoF/RR)
Lack of theoretical justification: why heterogeneous-group advantage estimation works in multi-agent settings relies entirely on empirical observation without formal analysis
Incomplete design space exploration: no ablations on group size G (fixed at 4), RR probabilities, or aggregation functions; sensitivity analysis absent
Unclear generalization: parameter sharing assumption may not hold for heterogeneous agents; backward reward propagation assumes tree/DAG structure; scalability to deeper/wider MAS unexplored
Reward modeling limitations: experiments use F1 score requiring gold-standard answers; agent-specific penalties are task-specific; applicability to other domains unclear
Out-of-domain generalization concerns: modest improvements on in-domain data, regression on MuSiQue suggests method may be overfit to HotpotQA characteristics
Reproducibility gaps: reference model update strategy not fully specified; no code availability mentioned; validation on only 500 samples
Missing failure mode analysis: when does MAPPO outperform MHGPO? What are fundamental limitations? Conditions for preferring MAPPO unexplored

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: critic networks indeed struggle with heterogeneous multi-agent outputs, and the motivation for critic-free alternatives is sound
Clear and detailed presentation: methodology is well-explained with effective visualizations (Figures 2-4) and comprehensive algorithm descriptions; reproducible implementation details provided
Solid empirical analysis on tested task: insightful analysis of heterogeneous→homogeneous group convergence (Figures 7-9), agent behavior evolution, and case studies demonstrating real improvements
Demonstrated computational efficiency: achieves lower memory usage and training time than MAPPO without critic networks; avoids SFT warm-up pretraining
Testing on multiple related datasets: evaluates on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue showing some generalization within QA domain
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution is applying existing GRPO to heterogeneous agent groups—an incremental extension. Backward reward propagation is straightforward. Heterogeneous group advantage estimation lacks theoretical justification and is only empirically validated on one task type

Severely limited experimental scope contradicts broad claims: despite claiming applicability to 'all MAS,' experiments cover only retrieval-augmented QA with fixed three-agent architecture (Rewriter-Reranker-Answerer), single backbone model (Llama3.1-8B), and single epoch training. Authors acknowledge 'detailed analysis...solely carried out on MASS...experiments on more scenarios reserved for future work'—undermining generality claims

Insufficient baseline comparisons: only MAPPO compared; missing DAPO (concurrent work), other MARL algorithms (QMIX, MADDPG), and simpler baselines. PPO baseline unexpectedly weak with no investigation

Critical missing ablations and design justifications: group size fixed at G=4 with no ablation; reward propagation uses simple averaging without justification; one-epoch training unjustified; no sensitivity analysis for learning rates (5e-7 to 1e-6) or RR probabilities (0.7, 0.1, 0.2); parameter-sharing assumption not discussed

Lack of statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing across any results; appears to be single runs; no multiple seeds reported; one-epoch training exacerbates variance but unanalyzed

No theoretical analysis: why heterogeneous group advantage estimation works is only empirically shown through diversity reduction. Convergence properties, theoretical guarantees, and general conditions for applicability not established. Claim that 'parameter sharing + reward backpropagation' enables heterogeneous groups remains intuitive assertion

Task-specific reward design limits generalization: penalties on query count, document redundancy, and answer length are custom-designed for QA; no guidance for designing rewards for other MAS types; severely undermines applicability claims
Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned; missing details on Wikipedia dump version, exact validation construction; generalization procedure to new MAS architectures unclear

Overstated generality claims: title and abstract suggest broad applicability to LLM-based MAS, but experiments contradict this. Out-of-domain tests (2Wiki, MuSiQue) are still QA variants, not different MAS types. Scalability (number of agents) unstudied beyond three-agent case

strengths: Clear problem motivation with well-articulated limitations of existing approaches (prompt engineering, MAPPO instability in MAS settings)
Novel application of group-based optimization to heterogeneous multi-agent settings with three thoughtful rollout sampling strategies
Comprehensive empirical analysis including convergence behavior, GPU memory efficiency, training time, and stability comparisons across three QA datasets
Insightful analysis of group diversity evolution during training (Figures 7-9) providing intuitive understanding of why the method works
Consistent practical improvements: 2x gain over unoptimized systems, lower memory usage, faster convergence without warm-up
Strong implementation transparency with detailed algorithms, reproducible hyperparameters, and clear experimental setup
Clear presentation with informative visualizations effectively communicating core concepts
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope undermines generalizability claims: tested on only one MAS architecture (three-agent search) and one task domain (multi-hop QA), contradicting abstract claims of broad applicability

Lacks formal theoretical justification for heterogeneous-group advantage estimation; explanation in Section 4 relies on post-hoc empirical observation rather than formal convergence or soundness proof
Incomplete baseline comparison: only MAPPO compared; no other recent MARL algorithms tested; missing standalone GRPO baseline and simpler alternatives
Limited training regime (1 epoch only) insufficient for strong conclusions; no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds
Heavy hand-crafting of agent-specific reward penalties contradicts end-to-end optimization narrative; no sensitivity analysis on reward design choices
Key design choices not ablated: group size G fixed at 4; hyperparameter sensitivity (learning rate, KL penalty) not explored; no ablation on backward propagation or aggregation operators
Generalization concerns: parameter sharing assumes single-LLM instantiation inappropriate for truly heterogeneous agents; claims about general MAS not supported beyond sequential architectures
Missing reproducibility details: code release not mentioned; exact prompt variations, Contriever setup, and corpus preprocessing not fully specified
No analysis of failure modes, limitations, or when method breaks down; unclear behavior on longer agent chains or non-sequential topologies
Some results show proposed method underperforming baseline (e.g., MHGPO-IS on 2WikiMultihopQA), yet this variant presented as contribution

strengths: Novel contribution as first systematic study of group-based optimization for multi-agent systems, with well-motivated heterogeneous-group advantage estimation to capture global system success rather than local agent performance
Solid theoretical framework with formal connections to single-context GRPO (Appendix D) and clear articulation of assumptions and their violations in practice
Multiple thoughtfully designed rollout sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR) with explicit efficiency-effectiveness trade-offs providing practical flexibility
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with three datasets, strong baselines, training dynamics analysis, computational cost tracking, and multiple ablations demonstrating consistent improvements
Clear evidence of practical improvements: smoother convergence, ~60% lower GPU memory than MAPPO, faster training while maintaining or improving task performance
Well-written paper with good intuition for why heterogeneous grouping works via progressive homogenization and global coordination pressure (Section 4.3)
weaknesses: Severely limited task scope: evaluation restricted to multi-hop QA with static retrieval; no assessment on planning, dynamic tool use, complex reasoning, or other coordination patterns substantially limits generality claims
Model scale gap: all experiments use Llama3.1-8B; behavior with larger models (70B+) is untested and critical for practical deployment claims in 2026
Fixed agent topology: only 3-agent linear pipeline tested; scalability to larger teams (5+ agents) and non-linear topologies remains unknown despite claimed generality

Significant theoretical gaps: (1) no formal variance analysis of heterogeneous grouping under partial observability despite intentional cross-trajectory coupling, (2) context-sufficiency assumption (A3) is strong and frequently violated with limited convergence analysis, (3) progressive homogenization (Figure 11) interpreted as task-specific convergence but paper acknowledges evidence does not rule out entropy collapse

Incomplete baseline comparisons: R1-Searcher uses different training setup making fairness unclear; MAPPO may be undertunked (only two learning rates tested); no comparison with other adapted GOA variants

Reward design dependency underexplored: format penalties appear critical but are task-specific (Table 4 shows F1 drops 49.5→44.0 without them); minimal guidance for generalizing to domains with harder reward functions
Statistical rigor: many results in Table 1 lack confidence intervals; overlapping intervals between MHGPO variants; no significance testing reported
Single epoch training only; convergence behavior and cumulative gains from multi-epoch training unknown; limited analysis of failure modes and when method underperforms

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem in optimizing multi-agent LLM systems with clear motivation
Comprehensive experimental analysis within scope, including helpful ablations (Tables 2-4), training dynamics (Figures 5-7), and case studies
Demonstrates notable computational efficiency gains over MAPPO (lower GPU memory and wall-clock time, Figure 6)
Well-designed exploration of efficiency-effectiveness trade-offs through three rollout sampling strategies
Detailed supplementary material with formal algorithms and theoretical analysis (Appendix D)
weaknesses: Core mechanism unclear: Figure 11 shows heterogeneous groups progressively homogenize during training, undermining the narrative that heterogeneous grouping is essential for capturing inter-agent dependencies

Severe scope limitations acknowledged: QA-only evaluation, fixed 3-agent systems, 8B-parameter ceiling, single-epoch training (176 steps)—these drastically constrain applicability and generalizability

Weak theoretical contribution: Propositions 1-3 rely on Assumption A3 (context sufficiency) that is acknowledged to be frequently violated in practice; no variance analysis of heterogeneous grouping under partial observability

Limited baseline comparisons: Only MAPPO is compared (a weak baseline for LLMs); no comparison to other MARL methods or alternative critic-free approaches; architectural differences with R1-Searcher make direct comparison unclear

Insufficient experimental validation: Single-epoch training is inadequate for assessing convergence; modest improvements (HotpotQA F1: +4.5% over MAPPO); no statistical significance testing; weak OOD generalization (26% vs. 43% F1)

Incomplete analysis of design choices: Reward aggregation ablation (Table 3) shows small differences; no analysis of why averaging is optimal; group size analysis (Table 6) lacks investigation into why performance saturates
Incremental novelty: Backward reward propagation is straightforward; heterogeneous grouping is conceptually simple; main contribution is engineering these together for multi-agent systems

Presentation issues: Core mechanism not clearly explained in Section 3.1; vague framing of 'implicit cross-trajectory relations'; key figures (3-4) appear mid-paper; progressive homogenization contradicts the heterogeneous grouping narrative

strengths: Novel problem formulation extending group-based optimization to multi-agent multi-context settings with clear motivation and technical soundness
Strong empirical results with 5x efficiency gains (49.9s vs 244.1s per step) and consistent F1 improvements across datasets; MHGPO-FoF(os) achieves 50.86% on HotpotQA vs 46.40% for MAPPO
Solid theoretical contributions formalizing connection to single-context GRPO through three propositions with rigorous proofs (Propositions 1-3)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including thorough ablations (Tables 2-4), training dynamics analysis (Figures 5-7), and detailed resource efficiency metrics

Clear technical approach combining backward reward propagation for capturing inter-agent dependencies with heterogeneous grouping for global system optimization; three sampling strategies represent meaningful trade-offs
Excellent reproducibility with detailed algorithms, hyperparameters, agent prompts, and implementation details in appendices
Strong practical value addressing real LLM deployment challenges with readily adoptable framework
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: QA-only (no other MASS domains), fixed 3-agent pipeline (no variable team sizes/topologies), up to 8B models only (no scaling to 70B+) - substantially undermines generalizability claims despite acknowledged in limitations

Strong theoretical assumption (A3: Context Sufficiency) may not hold broadly in practice; paper shows empirically it works when violated but provides no formal analysis of robustness under imperfect contexts
Missing variance analysis of heterogeneous grouping despite acknowledging 'additional variance in relative-reward signal'; no formal stability or convergence guarantees provided

Mechanistic understanding of why heterogeneous grouping works is insufficient; claims about 'down-weighting coordination-failure trajectories' lack rigorous justification; progressive homogenization (Figure 10) may explain gains but contribution unclear

Design choices lack principled justification: group size G chosen as 'trade-off' without principled selection guidance; RR probabilities {0.7,0.1,0.2} unjustified; agent-specific reward penalties appear hand-crafted
Entropy collapse risk acknowledged but not rigorously addressed; evidence in Section C.3 is only empirical without formal bounds
Incomplete baseline comparison: only MAPPO for multi-agent RL, no comparison with other recent critic-free MARL methods; R1-Searcher is single-context method so comparison limited
One case study (Figure 9) insufficient for understanding learned behaviors; OOD generalization (Table 1) weaker than ID but not analyzed
